## Why the best teams win
The model trained on 256 knockout team-seasons using group and league-phase stats achieves a mean within-season Spearman correlation of 0.46 between predicted and actual stages, while correctly ranking 46.7% of actual finalists in its top four of their respective seasons. Its predictive accuracy is reflected in a Brier score of 0.098 compared to the base-rate guess's 0.103, indicating an improvement over simply guessing based on historical frequencies without claiming statistical superiority. When analyzing which specific attributes drive deep runs, "Attacks per game" emerges as the most critical factor with an importance value of 0.25, followed by "Goal difference per game" at 0.201 and "Long passes (% of passes)" at 0.137. These top three statistics are all marked as robust, meaning a logistic model agrees on their direction in at least 12 of the 15 seasons analyzed, whereas other factors like "Fouls committed per game" or "Shot conversion" show lower importance values and varying levels of consistency.

Comparing feature sets reveals that the "style" category containing 12 stats yields a Spearman correlation of 0.41 and an AUC of 0.69, outperforming the single-stat "pedigree" set which only reaches 0.28 and 0.66 respectively. The combined "all" feature set achieves the highest performance with a Spearman of 0.46 and an AUC of 0.72, yet removing pedigree leaves the model nearly unchanged at 0.47 and 0.72, suggesting that historical reputation contributes less than on-pitch metrics. Conversely, excluding "results" drops the correlation to 0.40 while excluding "style" reduces it further to 0.37, highlighting that style-based statistics are more central to predicting knockout progression than past results or pedigree alone. SHAP contributions for these stats measure their push on the expected stage in knockout rounds, where a positive value indicates an upward shift and a negative one a downward shift, though this reflects model association rather than a causal strength of the team's profile.

## Winners vs runners-up
When comparing group and league-phase statistics between winners and runners-up across 15 finals, no single stat shows a statistically significant difference because every Holm-adjusted p-value remains above the significance threshold of 0.05. For instance, "Pre-season UEFA club coefficient" saw winners higher in 13 of 15 cases with a mean z-score difference of 0.57, yet its p-value of 0.111 indicates this pattern could easily occur by chance rather than reflecting a consistent advantage. Similarly, while winners committed fewer fouls in 12 finals compared to runners-up, the Holm-adjusted p of 0.181 means we cannot conclude that lower foul counts reliably predict victory over the long term based on this dataset. The analysis confirms that even when a winner ranks higher on a stat like "Shots per game" in 11 instances, the lack of statistical significance prevents us from asserting a definitive link between that specific metric and winning the final.

The data shows that winners were ranked higher than runners-up in terms of "Attacks per game" in 11 finals with a mean difference z-score of 0.9, yet this association still fails to reach the required p-value threshold for significance. In contrast, stats like "Points per game" and "Goal difference per game" show nearly identical distributions between winners and runners-up, with Holm-adjusted p-values of 1.0 indicating no discernible separation in performance during the group or league phases. Even though "Long passes (% of passes)" were lower for winners in 10 finals compared to just 5 where they were higher, the resulting p-value of 1.0 suggests this trend is not a reliable differentiator between the two groups. Ultimately, while certain stats like "Fouls committed per game" show directional trends where winners performed better, the statistical evidence does not support declaring any specific group/league-phase stat as a definitive driver of final outcomes.

Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Better than this %' figures say how many teams the club beat on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where beating a team means having the lower value. Write them as 'better than X% of teams', never as 'top X%'. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat or a team's profile drove, powered, propelled, carried, helped, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Write plain markdown without tables.

Write 350-450 words of markdown in total, two paragraphs of 3-4 sentences under each of exactly these two headings, in this order:
## Why the best teams win
## Winners vs runners-up

Explain which stats are associated with deep knockout runs and whether pedigree, results or style matters most, using the feature-set comparison. Say how well the model does by comparing its Brier score with the base-rate Brier score and stating how often finalists were in its top 4; the model's edge over the base-rate guess was not tested, so do not call it significant or superior. 'Importance' is the average size of a stat's push on the expected stage, in either direction. The model learns from the knockout team-seasons, using each team's group/league-phase stats. Only call a stat 'robust' if its robustness label is robust. Winners vs runners-up compares those same group/league-phase stats, not what happened in the final. Never call a winners-vs-runners-up difference significant unless its Holm-adjusted p is below the significance threshold in the facts.
